doc.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York years and Manhattan School
title: Being a studio musician or not
summary: He found studio work honest labour but chose to pursue his own music after working with Johnny Mathis.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Were you getting a lot of session work at this time?
Was that a–I’ve talked to some musicians who’ve found that a mixed blessing, was that the case with you?
No, I was grateful. It was honest work...
...and it was something I could do, and...it’s labor.

A love of labor. Um...of course...doing that kind of work is, is not creative in the sense of creating your personal kind of music, because you’re supposed to interpret whatever music they put in front of you. And if one is happy being a studio musician, and he’s good at it, it can make a really decent living.

And...but um one time I was trying to decide whether I should be a studio musician, ‘cause I was getting quite a bit of work. I was working at the Waldorf Astoria in the band, orchestra behind Johnny Mathis, et cetera, but then I decided I didn’t want to do that. I had, I thought I had something personal I wanted to express, so I kind of moved away from that.
